pip and venv, and why you have to activate

2026-11-02

While building this site I wrote a small Python script (build.py) that turns Markdown files into HTML. It depends on a single package, markdown, but when I ran python3 build.py I got an error:

ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'markdown'

even though I had already installed it. This post is what I learned from that.

What is pip?

pip downloads Python packages from a central repository called PyPI onto your machine.

pip install markdown

This downloads the markdown package and stores it in the site-packages folder of the Python that pip is attached to. When a script says import markdown, Python looks for it in that folder.

The key point: a package is installed for one particular Python, not for the whole machine.

The problem with installing everything globally

If you install everything into the machine's single Python, you run into trouble:

  • Project A needs version 1 of a package and project B needs version 2, but one Python can only hold one version.
  • Old packages you no longer use pile up, and you can't tell which project they belong to.
  • Some systems (for example Python installed through Homebrew on macOS) refuse outright and answer error: externally-managed-environment, because they don't want you changing packages the system itself depends on.

What is venv?

venv creates a second, separate copy of Python inside your project folder, with its own place to store packages.

python3 -m venv .venv
.venv/bin/pip install markdown

The first line creates the .venv/ folder. The second installs markdown into the Python inside .venv, not the system one. Each project gets its own set of packages, so they can't collide.

Why do you have to activate it?

This was the part that confused me most. The python3 you type in the terminal is the machine's Python, and it knows nothing about .venv/. So there are three ways to end up using the Python in .venv:

Command Python that runs Finds markdown?
python3 build.py the system's no
.venv/bin/python build.py the one in .venv yes
source .venv/bin/activate, then python build.py the one in .venv yes

activate isn't magic. It just makes the word python in that terminal point to the Python inside .venv, and only for that terminal window. Open a new window and you have to do it again. deactivate undoes it.

Which should you use?

venv trades a cleaner machine for extra steps when you run things.

  • Several projects, or many packages: use venv. Version conflicts are real and painful to untangle.
  • One project, few packages, on your own machine: a plain pip install into the machine's Python is fine, as long as your system doesn't block it.

I chose venv for this site because that's the usual best practice, but it turned out to be slightly more than I needed, since there is one project and one package.

If you don't want to type the long command every time

  • Use .venv/bin/python build.py directly, with no activation.
  • Let the script find the venv itself. In this site's build.py, if markdown is missing, the script creates .venv, installs it, and re-runs itself with the .venv Python. The result is that python3 build.py works as normal.
  • Tools like uv manage the venv for you automatically (I haven't tried it yet).

Things to remember

  • Always put .venv/ in .gitignore. Don't commit it.
  • Keep your package list in a requirements.txt (create it with pip freeze > requirements.txt). Other people, or you in the future, can then install everything with pip install -r requirements.txt.
  • If you get ModuleNotFoundError even though you installed the package, suspect first that the Python running your script and the Python pip installed into are two different ones. Check with which python3 and python3 -m pip --version.

python pip venv
